title: The Leidenfrost effect
hook: Water lasts longer on a very hot pan than on one that is merely hot.
peek: Flick water onto a warm pan and it boils away fast. Flick it onto a much hotter one and the drops skate around for a minute or more, floating on a thin cushion of their own steam.
lede: Drop water on a pan at about 100 degrees Celsius and it fizzes away in seconds. Heat the pan to around 200 degrees or more and something odd happens: the water beads up into shiny balls that glide about and can last a minute or more. The underside of each drop boils so fast that it lifts the drop on a layer of vapour.

bullets.text: The German doctor Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost described the effect in 1756, in a book about the qualities of water. He placed drops on a red-hot iron spoon and timed how long they lasted.

The layer of steam under the drop is only a fraction of a millimetre thick, but vapour carries heat poorly. So the drop is shielded from the very surface that should boil it, and evaporates far more slowly.

The temperature where the effect starts is called the Leidenfrost point. For water on a metal pan it is somewhere around 200 degrees Celsius, though it shifts with the surface, its roughness and the liquid.
Some cooks use the effect to check a stainless steel pan. When flicked water forms rolling beads instead of sizzling away, the pan is hot enough for food to sear and stick less.
In 2006 physicists showed that drops on a hot surface cut with sawtooth ridges travel in one direction by themselves, and can even roll slightly uphill.
